Hey so you can read what I wrote here but I also need you to clarify the final question (about sending the atom back in time, I'm not sure I get the question):

This is a very interesting question. I'm not sure how well I can answer it but I will give it a shot.

First, General Relativity does not explain WHY things have mass. It just explains how things with mass interact with each other. In general, this means that the question you've asked is not within the scope of GR. So what is mass exactly?

We now have good evidence that the Higgs Boson exists as predicted by Peter Higgs. The Higgs Field is a theoretical field of Higgs particles that interact with the familiar particles of particle physics. Thus, an electron has less mass than a proton, simply because it has a weaker interaction with the Higgs Field.

So the mass of a particle is just the strength of interaction with the Higgs Field, similar to how charge is the strength of interaction with an electromagnetic field. In my understanding, any physical interaction requires time to be moving forward (or simply entropy must be increasing). However the strength of an interaction is defined instantaneously. Philosophically this would imply that mass is localized in the present moment. If time were to freeze, the Higgs interaction would stop and you would not be able to measure the mass of anything. Similarly, a particle's total mass can only be defined as that same instantaneous mass (rather than what I think you are asking which is if we'd sum this mass over the time that particle existed.)

I'm not quite sure about the end of your question but I'd love to hear if this helped at all.

In order to determine the particle position Einstein's four-dimensional universe, it is not sufficient to know the six independent partial differential equations that they must fulfill; one needs also to know the conditions at the boundaries of the Universe, which are necessary for specializing the integrals in view of given problems.

These boundary conditions are of two sorts. One deals with the far away state of the Universe, completely outside the region where we wish to study the events; it is the one whose choice, still in dispute, is translated into this question: is the Universe infinite? Is it finite, although without limit? I do not bother with this here.

The other one deals with the singular lines that correspond to what, from the experimental viewpoint, we call the attractive masses. In Newtonian gravitation the material point of mass m corresponds to the point of the Euclidean space where the integral of Laplace's equation becomes infinite like m/r, where r is (in the neighborhood of this point) the distance from the material point to the point where one studies the Newtonian potential. It is this kind of singularities, characteristic of matter, that make the difference.

In the present state of our experimental knowledge, nothing entitles us to suppose that singular points (in four dimensions) may exist in the Universe. From the analytical viewpoint, this impossibility is evidently connected with the distinction that exists between one of the variables and the remaining three, which allows for the sign changes, like in acoustics.
